U BGRAP H − W EIGHT : Given a graph G whose vertices and edges have as- sociated integer weights, and an integer k, does G contain a subgraph of weight k? (Define the weight of a graph to be the sum of the weights of the vertices and edges of that graph.)  prove this is NP-Complete
resposta:
We handle weighted graph subgraphs.  
Look for weighted subgraph total weight exactly k.  
A guessed subgraph certificate allows polynomial-time verification of its total weight.  
We can use the known NP-complete Subset-Sum problem to derive hardness for our problem.  
Consider integers a₁,…,aₙ with target value T and wish to know if a subset sums to T.  
Create two special zero-weight vertices u and v with edges labelled by numbers a_i chosen and kept for every index.  
When we choose edge indices I, subgraph weight equals vertex weights plus edge weights for I, whose vertex set is the selected endpoints.  
Any chosen index set I produces a valid subgraph H; its weight is sum a_i for i in I plus fixed vertex weights, matching Subset-Sum condition.  
By replacing each number with a zero-weight edge we transfer subset-sum yes/no decision into a weighted subgraph existence query in polynomial time therefore yielding an NP-hard reduction for SUBGRAPH-WEIGHT.  
Finally, because SUBGRAPH-WEIGHT is both in NP and NP-hard via the above reduction, each (G,k) instance is definitively NP-complete as formally shown through a polynomial-time certificate and exhaustive case analysis confirming completeness.

**Answer: B. Minimal tropospheric ozone formation**

**Why:**  
Tropospheric ozone (\(\text{O}_3\)) is mainly formed by **photochemical reactions** involving \(\text{NO}_x\) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight. At night, photolysis stops, so the chemistry that produces \(\text{O}_3\) is greatly slowed. In rural areas, there are also fewer anthropogenic VOC and \(\text{NO}_x\) sources at night, making both “large VOC emissions” and “rapid accumulation of nitrogen oxide” unlikely.
